nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong year-round sun drives algae and seagrass growth in the clear shallows and warms the sand where turtle eggs incubate.

nodes.name: Monsoon upwelling
nodes.desc: Summer monsoon winds draw nutrient-rich water to the surface of the Arabian Sea, making it one of the most productive seas on Earth.

nodes.name: Tidal lagoons (khaurs)
nodes.desc: Lagoons such as Khaur Jarama have mudflats, scattered mangroves and fish nursery habitat, and feed wintering waders.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Microbes and scavenging invertebrates break down dead animals, eggs and plant matter, returning nutrients to sand and lagoon.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting microscopic algae that bloom when monsoon upwelling brings nutrients up; the base of the open-water food chain.

nodes.name: Seagrass
nodes.desc: Seagrass meadows in warm shallow water are the main food of adult green turtles, and shelter young fish.

nodes.name: Sea lettuce
nodes.desc: A green seaweed of rocky and shallow shores that green turtles are recorded grazing.

nodes.name: Grey mangrove
nodes.desc: Salt-tolerant tree that grows in scattered stands in the lagoons, where it stabilises mud and shelters young fish and crabs.

nodes.name: Copepods
nodes.desc: Tiny crustaceans that graze phytoplankton and are in turn eaten by small fish.

nodes.name: Indian oil sardine
nodes.desc: A schooling fish of the Arabian Sea that feeds on plankton and is a key prey fish for birds, dolphins and larger fish.

nodes.name: Green turtle
nodes.desc: Adults graze seagrass and algae; females nest on the beaches of Ras al Jinz and Ras al Hadd year-round. The reserve is among the world's most important green turtle nesting sites.

nodes.name: Dromedary
nodes.desc: Domestic camels graze and browse coastal shrubs and mangroves along the Arabian coast; a few records fall in the circle.

nodes.name: Ghost crab
nodes.desc: Burrowing beach crabs that hunt and scavenge at night; crabs are among the predators of turtle hatchlings crossing the sand.

nodes.name: Crab-plover
nodes.desc: A wader with a heavy bill specialised for eating crabs; it nests in burrows in sandy banks around the Arabian Sea.

nodes.name: Sooty gull
nodes.desc: A very commonly recorded gull on this coast. Gulls are known to take turtle hatchlings as they crawl to the sea.

nodes.name: Great crested tern
nodes.desc: A fish-eating tern that plunge-dives for small schooling fish along the shore.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: A fish-eating raptor that hunts by diving; commonly recorded along this coast.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: An opportunistic predator and scavenger; red foxes are known to dig up and eat sea turtle eggs.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: A large shark and the main natural predator of sea turtles of all sizes.

nodes.name: Indian Ocean humpback dolphin
nodes.desc: A shallow coastal dolphin that feeds on fish, squid and crustaceans, with important populations along the Arabian Peninsula.
